message.content:
Aluminum is the better conductor, but staying hot is a different job. It comes down to how much heat the metal can hold, which is its mass multiplied by how much heat each pound absorbs. Per pound, aluminum actually holds more heat than iron. Per cubic inch, the two are close. So the deciding factor is simply how much metal is in the pan.

A 10-inch cast-iron skillet usually weighs about 4 to 5 pounds. A thin aluminum pan of the same size may weigh well under a pound. The skillet carries several times more stored heat at the same temperature.

Picture both pans preheated to the same temperature, then two cold, damp steaks laid in each. The thin aluminum pan gives up its small reserve almost at once, and its surface temperature falls fast. Juices pool instead of evaporating, and the steaks start to steam. The skillet dips too, but less, because it has so much heat to spend, so the surface stays hot enough to keep browning.

Conductivity plays a different role. It governs how quickly heat spreads across the pan, which is why aluminum heats fast and cast iron feels slow.

The comparison has a limit: it assumes thin aluminum. A thick, heavy aluminum pan can hold heat nearly as well as cast iron.
